chunks: Kuki AI Agent Overview Link to Kuki: https://chatgpt.com/g/g-6887621fc0ac8191933b2bcfba73a075-kuki Kuki is an AI educational tutor created to support students at USIU-A in their academic journey. The agent is designed to answer questions, explain concepts, and summarize coursework using only the uploaded course notes and knowledge base. Kuki functions as a reliable study partner, focusing on accuracy, clarity, and accessibility for students. Use Case: Educational Tutor Goal: Help students understand, revise, and engage with their coursework. Subjects Covered: Information Literacy Linear Algebra Discrete Mathematics Differential Equations Optimization Techniques Design and Implementation Framework: ChatGPT integrated within an open-source orchestration layer such as LangChain. Knowledge Source: Lecture notes and academic materials provided by students. System Instructions: Kuki only provi

des answers drawn directly from the uploaded documents. If information is not available in the documents, Kuki responds clearly: “Sorry, but I can’t seem to get the answer to that right now.” Interaction Style: The agent communicates in a supportive, clear, and student-focused manner. Features Contextual Responses: Provides answers strictly based on the uploaded course material. Guidance Options: Offers either concise summaries or step-by-step explanations depending on the student’s preference. Visual Support: Breaks down complex concepts into formulas, tables, or diagrams where needed. Ethical Safeguards: Does not guess or generate information outside the provided notes. Acknowledges limitations when answers are unavailable. Maintains transparency about the source of information. Example Interaction Student: “Can you explain eigenvalues in Linear Algebra?” Kuki: Summarizes the definitio

n of eigenvalues, provides the formula, and explains the concept using the uploaded Linear Algebra notes. Student: “What if the information is not in the notes?” Kuki: “Sorry, but I can’t seem to get the answer to that right now.” Limitations Knowledge is limited to the uploaded documents. Cannot access live internet sources or external databases. Not intended to replace lecturers or professional tutors. Future Improvements To make Kuki more effective and widely accessible to USIU-A students, several improvements are planned: Platform Expansion Integrate Kuki into WhatsApp, where most students already interact daily. Embed Kuki on the official USIU-A website for easy access. Integrate Kuki into a future official school mobile application if developed. Feedback and Iteration Create a structured feedback system to collect student experiences and suggestions. Use the feedback to continuousl

y refine Kuki’s answers, tone, and usefulness. Enhanced Knowledge Base Continuously update Kuki’s knowledge with new course notes, assignments, and approved learning resources. Expand subject coverage beyond the initial five courses. Personalization Allow Kuki to tailor responses based on a student’s academic year, enrolled courses, or preferred learning style. Integration with Academic Services Connect Kuki to academic calendars, deadlines, and announcements to provide reminders and alerts. Offer links to official university resources such as the library, registrar’s office, or counselling services.

chunks: Agents & Environment Week2 Objective By the end of this lesson, the learner should be able to understand the concept of intelligent agents, the role of environments in AI systems, and how intelligent agents interact with and adapt to their environments. Learning Outcomes Demonstrate an understanding of the fundamental concepts of intelligent agents including their characteristics and types Categorize and analyze environments in the context of AI systems Analyze how intelligent agents modify their behavior in response to changing environments. Higher Education Learn to BUILD MODELS (using differential equations, statistical probabilities, physical and computational simulations,) that we can use to EXPLAIN the Past, PREDICT the future, UNDERSTAND the subject, and CONTROL the world In AI, we build models of THINKING, AI Building machine models targeted at THINKING PERCEPTION ACTION In order

to have a model, you MUST have a REPRESENTATION AI is about building Methods, Algorithms, Representations that support the building of models that are intelligent ( i.e. facilitate an understanding of thinking, perception, and action) Overview: Fundamental AI Concepts Intelligent Agents: entities that perceive their environment and take actions to achieve goals. Intelligent agents make decisions based on their observations, adapting to changing situations. Problem solving: involves finding solutions to complex issues. Search algorithms, heuristics, and optimization techniques are essential components of problem-solving in AI. Knowledge Representation and Reasoning: involves organizing information in a way that AI systems can utilize. Reasoning allows AI systems to draw conclusions and make decisions based on the represented knowledge. Machine Learning: a subset of AI that focuses on cre

ating algorithms and models that enable computers to learn from data and improve their performance over time. This includes supervised learning, unsupervised learning, and reinforcement learning. Neural Networks and Deep Learning: computational models inspired by the human brain. Deep learning, a subset of machine learning, involves training deep neural networks to perform tasks such as image recognition and natural language processing. Natural Language Processing (NLP): enables computers to understand, interpret, and generate human language. It encompasses tasks like sentiment analysis, language translation, and speech recognition. AI Concepts Search Algorithms: are used to navigate through problem spaces and find solutions efficiently. Algorithms like depth-first search, breadth-first search, and A* are commonly employed in AI Expert Systems: Expert systems mimic the decision-making ca

pabilities of a human expert in a specific domain. They use rule-based systems and knowledge bases to provide expert-level advice. Computer vision: involves enabling machines to interpret and understand visual information from the world, such as image and video recognition Robotics: involves the design, creation, and operation of robots to perform tasks autonomously. It integrates computer vision, machine learning, and control systems. Ethics in AI: address the responsible development and use of AI technologies, including issues related to bias, transparency, accountability, and the societal impact of AI. 271- Fall 2006 Agents An agent is anything that can be viewed as perceiving its environment through sensors and acting upon that environment through actuators Human agent: eyes, ears, and other organs for sensors; hands, legs, mouth, and other body parts for actuators Hardware Agents (a

utonomous Robots) : cameras and infrared range finders for sensors;various motors for actuators Software Agents: comprise a program that calculates a result from user input 271- Fall 2006 Agents and environments The agent function maps from percept histories to actions: [f: P*  A] The agent program runs on the physical architecture to produce f agent = architecture + program Sensors: What detects the changes and events in the environment Actuators/ Effectors: Movable parts of an Agent Perception: a way in which something is understood or interpreted. Vacuum-cleaner Robot Intelligent Agents An intelligent agent is an autonomous entity which act upon an environment using sensors and actuators for achieving goals. An intelligent agent may learn from the environment to achieve their goals. A thermostat is an example of an intelligent agent. Rule 1: An AI agent must have the ability to perce

ive the environment. Rule 2: The observation must be used to make decisions. Rule 3: Decision should result in an action. Rule 4: The action taken by an AI agent must be a rational action. 271- Fall 2006 Rational agents A rational agent is an agent which has clear preference, models uncertainty, and acts in a way to maximize its performance measure with all possible actions. An agent should strive to "do the right thing", based on what it can perceive and the actions it can perform. The right action is the one that will cause the agent to be most successful Performance measure: An objective criterion for success of an agent's behavior in the environment E.g., performance measure of a vacuum-cleaner agent could be amount of dirt cleaned up, amount of time taken, amount of electricity consumed, amount of noise generated, etc. 271- Fall 2006 Rational agents Rational Agent: For each possible

percept sequence, a rational agent should select an action that is expected to maximize its performance measure, given the evidence provided by the percept sequence and whatever built-in knowledge the agent has. 271- Fall 2006 What’s involved in Intelligence? Intelligent agents Ability to interact with the real world to perceive, understand, and act e.g., speech recognition and understanding and synthesis e.g., image understanding e.g., ability to take actions, have an effect Knowledge Representation, Reasoning and Planning modeling the external world, given input solving new problems, planning and making decisions ability to deal with unexpected problems, uncertainties Learning and Adaptation we are continuously learning and adapting our internal models are always being “updated” e.g. a baby learning to categorize and recognize animals 271- Fall 2006 Implementing agents Table look-ups

docs.name: Week 4 Search Algorithms.pptx
chunks: Search Algorithms Lesson Learning Outcomes Differentiate between uninformed and informed search algorithms Discuss the characteristics, advantages and limitations of each type of search algorithm Analyze and identify appropriate search algorithms for specific problem-solving scenarios in the context of artificial intelligence. Apply search algorithms to solve real-world problems Lesson objectives Define the importance of search algorithms in AI for problem solving Types of search algorithms Exploration vs Exploitation Problem-solving agents Search techniques are universal problem-solving methods. Rational agents or Problem-solving agents in AI mostly use these search strategies or algorithms to solve a specific problem and provide the best result. Problem-solving agents are the goal-based agents and use atomic representation. What is a Search Algorithm? A search algorithm is a kind of al

gorithm used in artificial intelligence that explores a set of potential solutions, also known as a search space, in order to discover the best or most optimum solution to a problem. To identify the optimum answer for a given set of constraints, a search algorithm sorts through a vast number of options. Generally, search algorithms work by arranging the search space into a specific kind of graph, which is usually a tree, and then calculating the optimal score, or cost, of going through each branch of the tree. A path that maximizes the cost within the constraints of the implemented method from the start state to the goal state is called a solution. Components of a Search Problem State/Search Space The set of all possible states the system can be in. Each state represents a specific configuration or situation of the problem Initial/Start State It is a state from where an agent begins the

search. Goal State The desired state/condition that the system aims to reach. The objective of the search is to find a sequence of actions that lead from initial state to the goal state Operators/Actions The set of actions or operators that the system can perform to transition from one state to another. (building blocks of the search process) Transition model Describes how the system moves from one state to another when a specific action is applied. Path Cost The cost associated with taking a specific path. The goal is to find the path with minimum cost 6 Other Terms Search tree: A tree representation of search problem. The root of the search tree is the root node which is corresponding to the initial state. Time and space complexity are measured in ‘b‘ – maximum branching factor of the search tree. ‘d‘ – the depth of the least-cost solution. ‘m‘ – maximum depth of the state space(maybe

infinity) Solution: It is an action sequence which leads from the start node to the goal node. Optimal Solution: If a solution has the lowest cost among all solutions. ROBOTIC LAWN MOWER PROBLEM Define the problem Create a search space with states and actions Employ search algorithms Consider heuristics and optimization criteria Adapt to a dynamic environment, possibly with a learning mechanism 8 2/2/2024 9 2/2/2024 10 4 Essential Properties of Search Algorithms Completeness: A search algorithm is said to be complete if it guarantees to return a solution if at least any solution exists for any random input Optimality: If a solution found for an algorithm is guaranteed to be the best solution (lowest path cost) among all other solutions, then such a solution for is said to be an optimal solution. Time Complexity: Time complexity is a measure of time for an algorithm to complete its task.

Space Complexity: It is the maximum storage space required at any point during the search, as the complexity of the problem. 2/2/2024 AI: Chapter 3: Solving Problems by Searching 12 What is Uninformed Search in AI? Aka blind search : an algorithm that explores a problem space (produces the search tree ) without any domain knowledge or information about the problem other than the initial state and the possible actions to take. The machine blindly follows the algorithm regardless of whether right or wrong, efficient or in-efficient. (it’s brute force in nature) They systematically explore the search space for all possible solutions of the problem by applying predefined rules to generate successor states until a goal state is found or the search is exhausted. They are less efficient than informed search algorithms. They are used in various applications, ranging from game playing to route pl

anning and problem-solving Breadth-First Search (BFS) Exploration Strategy: Explores the search space level by level, visiting all nodes at the current level before moving on to the next level. Memory Usage: Requires more memory as it needs to store all nodes at the current level. Completeness: Guarantees finding the shallowest solution, making it complete if the branching factor is finite. Optimality: Finds the optimal solution in terms of the number of steps but not necessarily in terms of cost. Depth-First Search (DFS) Exploration Strategy: Explores as far as possible along one branch before backtracking. Memory Usage: Uses less memory compared to BFS, as it only needs to store the nodes along the current path. Completeness: May not be complete if the search space has infinite depth or loops. Optimality: Does not guarantee finding the optimal solution in terms of the number of steps o

r cost. Depth-Limited Search (DLS) Exploration Strategy: Similar to DFS but with a depth limit, preventing it from going too deep into the search space. Memory Usage: Uses less memory compared to DFS but may still require significant memory for deep searches. Completeness: Complete if the depth limit is greater than or equal to the depth of the optimal solution. Optimality: May not find the optimal solution if the depth limit is too shallow. Uniform-Cost Search (UCS) Exploration Strategy: Explores the least-cost path first, prioritizing nodes with lower path costs. Memory Usage: Can use a significant amount of memory, especially in scenarios with high path costs. Completeness: Complete if the step cost is greater than or equal to some small positive value and the solution exists. Optimality: Guarantees finding the optimal solution in terms of cost. Iterative deepening depth-first Search

Bidirectional Search Algorithm Completeness: Bidirectional Search is complete if we use BFS in both searches. Time Complexity: Time complexity of bidirectional search using BFS is O(bd). Space Complexity: Space complexity of bidirectional search is O(bd). Optimal: Bidirectional search is Optimal. Summary What is Informed Search in AI? AKA heuristic search: it use additional knowledge or heuristics to guide the search process Examples of additional knowledge: how far we are from the goal, path cost, how to reach to goal node, etc. This knowledge help agents to explore less to the search space and find more efficiently the goal node. (more useful for large search space) Heuristic is a function h(n) in Informed Search, used to find the most promising path. It takes the current state of the agent as its input and produces the estimation of how close agent is from the goal. Best-first Search

Algorithm (Greedy Search) Time Complexity: The worst case time complexity of Greedy best first search is O(bm). Space Complexity: The worst case space complexity of Greedy best first search is O(bm). Where, m is the maximum depth of the search space. Complete: Greedy best-first search is also incomplete, even if the given state space is finite. Optimal: Greedy best first search algorithm is not optimal. A* Search Algorithm A* search is the most commonly known form of best-first search. It uses heuristic function h(n), and cost to reach the node n from the start state g(n). A* algorithm returns the path which occurred first, and it does not search for all remaining paths. The efficiency of A* algorithm depends on the quality of heuristic. A* algorithm expands all nodes which satisfy the condition f(n) Key Features of Informed Search Applications of Search Algorithms Pathfinding: finding t

he shortest path between two points. Dijkstra's algorithm or A* (A-star) Scheduling Tasks efficiently: find an optimal schedule that minimizes the overall completion time. Game theory: enable players or AI agents to analyze potential moves, evaluate outcomes, and make informed decisions. References https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OmOwj3qMdOY https://angeluriot.com/maze_solver/ Top 5 Most Common Graph Algorithms for Coding Interviews (youtube.com) Breadth First Search (BFS): Visualized and Explained (youtube.com) Depth First Search (DFS) Explained: Algorithm, Examples, and Code (youtube.com)

chunks: Knowledge Representation in AI Week 5 Edward Ombui, PhD Lesson objective By the end of this lesson, students should be able to understand the importance of knowledge representation in artificial intelligence, explore different techniques, and apply these techniques to model information in a meaningful way. Lesson Learning Outcomes Articulate the advantages and challenges associated with different knowledge representation structures, including facts, rules, frames, semantic networks, ontologies, and knowledge graphs. Create meaningful knowledge representations for given scenarios by exploring semantic networks and frames. Identify real-world AI applications that integrate knowledge representation e..g. natural language processing, expert systems, and other domains. Powers of Ten™ (1977) HOW DO I KNOW? Ontology: What is REALITY? What is TRUTH? Epistemology: The theory of knowledge (and jus

tification) Knowledge: Belief connected with the fact known in the right way Knowledge is always of truths or realities; DEEP TRUTH Belief is not knowledge but opinion Justified belief: you have good reason to believe what you do, even if the belief is wrong Does knowledge begin with experience? (experience gives us data about observable level) Source of knowing: Scientifically (by observation and experimentation, and predictability of observables) CONCEPTS for building AI The role of logic in knowledge representation and reasoning Logic, the study of entailment relations: languages, truth conditions, and rules of inference Predicate calculus: : the language of first order logic (FOL). KNOWLEDGE REPRESENTATION REASONING What is Knowledge? Knowledge is awareness or familiarity gained by experiences of facts, data, and situations. We make decision about what to do based on what we know abo

ut the world Knowledge representation is the part of AI concerned with how an agent uses what it knows in deciding what to do. KR: the study of thinking as a computational process, and the symbolic structures invented to represent knowledge Types of Knowledge What is knowledge representation? A process of organizing information in a structured way to facilitate reasoning, problem-solving, and decision-making within intelligent systems It involves creating models that capture the essential characteristics of a domain, allowing an AI system to understand, interpret, and manipulate knowledge effectively. The goal of knowledge representation is to enable machines to reason about the world in a manner similar to human cognition. What to Represent Object: All the facts about objects in our world domain. E.g., Guitars contains strings, trumpets are brass instruments. Events: Events are the acti

ons which occur in our world. Performance: It describe behavior which involves knowledge about how to do things. Meta-knowledge: It is knowledge about what we know. Facts: Facts are the truths about the real world and what we represent. Knowledge-Base: The central component of the knowledge-based agents is the knowledge base. It is represented as KB. The Knowledgebase is a group of the Sentences (Here, sentences are used as a technical term and not identical with the English language). Early Systems Knowledge: Permissible Transformations Reasoning: Search Algorithm Issues Real world data is challenging Lack of generalization to large number of symbols No learning Recent Work Speech recogmition Image recognition Deep Neural networks Real valued vector (distributed representations) Transformation from input to output is learned from data using backpropagation algorithm Continuous data proc

essing through real numbers Related work in reasoning Natural Language Inference Visual Question Answering Reading Comprehension Knowledge Representation Schemes Relational Inheritable Inferential Declarative/Procedural Simple Relational Knowledge It’s the simplest way to represent facts, each set out systematically in columns It stores set of attributes and its associated values This approach of knowledge representation is popular in database systems where the relationship between different entities is represented Inheritable knowledge Here, all the data must be stored in a hierarchy of classes Inheritance property is applied whereby elements inherit values from other members of a class It shows the relation between an instance and class (instance relation) Every frame can represent the collection of attributes and its values Objects and values are represented in boxed nodes Inferential

Knowledge This represents knowledge in the form of formal logic This approach can be used to derive more facts and guarantees correctness Example: Given two statements Sudanese are tall Akuec is Sudanese This is represented as: sudanese(Akuec) Procedural Knowledge This uses software programs and codes to describe HOW to do specific things This approach uses the If-Then rule Example coding languages include LISP and Prolog languages We can easily represent heuristic or domain-specific knowledge using this approach However, not necessary to represent all cases using this approach Cycle of Knowledge Representation in AI AI Systems consist of various components to display their intelligent behavior. Some of these components include: Perception Learning Knowledge Representation & Reasoning Planning Execution Knowledge Representation Structures Facts: Simple statements about the world. Rules:

Statements that specify relationships or conditions. Frames: Structures that organize knowledge about objects or concepts. Semantic Networks: Graph structures representing relationships between entities. Ontologies: Hierarchical structures defining concepts and their relationships. Knowledge Graphs: Graph databases that connect entities and their relationships. chunks: Knowledge Representation & Reasoning in AI Week 6 Edward Ombui, PhD Lesson objective By the end of this lesson, students should be able to understand the concepts of knowledge representation and reasoning using semantic networks and frames, and apply these concepts to solve problems in AI. Lesson Learning Outcomes Explain the concepts of semantic networks and frames as knowledge representation structures in AI Demonstrate the ability to create semantic networks and frames to represent information in various domains. Demonstrate reasoning skills by performing inference and deduction tasks using semantic networks and frames. Knowledge Representation and Reasoning (KRR) KRR is the part of Artificial intelligence which concerned with AI agents thinking and how thinking contributes to intelligent behavior of agents. It is responsible for representing information about the real world so that a

computer can understand and can utilize this knowledge to solve the complex real world problems E.g. diagnosis a medical condition communicating with humans in natural language. It is also a way which describes how we can represent knowledge in artificial intelligence. Knowledge representation is not just storing data into some database, but it also enables an intelligent machine to learn from that knowledge and experiences so that it can behave intelligently like a human. Knowledge Representation Structures Facts: Simple statements about the world. Rules: Statements that specify relationships or conditions. Frames: Structures that organize knowledge about objects or concepts. Semantic Networks: Graph structures representing relationships between entities. Ontologies: Hierarchical structures defining concepts and their relationships. Knowledge Graphs: Graph databases that connect entiti

es and their relationships. Logic Representation Advantages of Logical Representation Logical representation enables us to do logical reasoning. Logical representation is the basis for the programming languages. Disadvantages Logical representations have some restrictions and are challenging to work with. Logical representation technique may not be very natural, and inference may not be so efficient. Propositional Logic A proposition is a declarative statement which is either true or false. It’s a technique of knowledge representation in logical nad mathematical form Example: It is Monday The Sun rises from North 2+4 <5 3 is a prime number. Propositional Logic Propositional logic is also called Boolean logic as it works on 0 and 1. In propositional logic, we use symbolic variables to represent the logic, and we can use any symbol for a representing a proposition, such A, B, C, P, Q, R, e

tc. Propositions can be either true or false, but it cannot be both. Propositional logic consists of an object, relations or function, and logical connectives. These connectives are also called logical operators. The propositions and connectives are the basic elements of the propositional logic. Connectives can be said as a logical operator which connects two sentences. A proposition formula which is always true is called tautology, and it is also called a valid sentence. A proposition formula which is always false is called Contradiction. Example A: It is hot B: It is humid C: It is raining Condition: If it is humid, then it is hot [Preposition :B ‐‐>A ] If it is hot and humid then it is not raining [Preposition: A ∩ B ‐‐>C Limitations of Propositional Logic We cannot represent relations like ALL, some, or none with propositional logic. Example: All the girls are intelligent. Some apple

s are sweet. Propositional logic has limited expressive power. In propositional logic, we cannot describe statements in terms of their properties or logical relationships. Semantic Network A visual and intuitive knowledge representation technique consisting of a network of nodes (representing concepts, objects or entities) connected by edges (representing relationships or links). Example: Following are some statements which we need to represent in the form of nodes and arcs. Visualizing Semantic Networks https://www.visuwords.com Advantages and Disadvantages Advantages Semantic networks are a natural representation of knowledge. Semantic networks convey meaning in a transparent manner. These networks are simple and easily understandable Disadvantages take more computational time at runtime it is not possible to build a vast semantic network to model human like memory they do not have any

equivalent quantifier, e.g., for all, for some, none, etc do not have any standard definition for the link names Are not intelligent and depend on the creator of the system Exercise Problem: Using a group of 5 to 7 friends who have different hobbies and interests, create a semantic network to represent the relationships between your friends and their hobbies. Use Nodes to represent each friend, while their hobbies will be connected to them as linked nodes. Each link will represent the relationship between the person and their hobbies. Example Information: John likes playing soccer and basketball. Sarah enjoys reading books and painting. Michael is interested in photography and hiking. Emily's hobbies include playing the guitar and cooking. David likes swimming and playing video games. Frames A frame is a data structure used to represent objects, concepts, or entities in a structured and

organized manner. Frames are derived from semantic networks and later evolved into our modern-day classes and objects. A frame consists of slots (also known as attributes or properties) and fillers (also known as values) associated with those slots. Each slot represents a specific aspect or characteristic of the object or concept being represented, and the fillers are the values associated with those characteristics. Facets are features of frames which enable us to put constraints on the frames. A frame is also known as slot-filter knowledge representation in artificial intelligence. Application: expert systems, natural language understanding, and automated reasoning. Advantages and Disadvantages Advantages The frame knowledge representation makes the programming easier by grouping the related data or knowledge (OOP) The frame representation is comparably flexible and used by many appli

cations in AI. It is very easy to add slots for new attribute and relations. [Flexibility] It is easy to include default data and to search for missing values. Frame representation is easier to understand and visualize than logic or rules Disadvantages In frame system inference mechanism is not be easily processed. Inference mechanism cannot be smoothly proceeded by frame representation. Frame representation has a much generalized approach.
